public_rationale: Marcus said some popular image generators had trained on copyrighted images. In the UK Getty Images v Stability AI case, Stability AI admitted that at least some of Getty's copyright works were used to train Stable Diffusion v2.0, and that sample works were used to train v1.4, v2.x and the SD XL models. All of these were released before January 2024. The judgment also notes it is common ground that Stable Diffusion was trained on the web-scraped LAION-5B dataset. Stable Diffusion was one of the most widely used image generators. So the claim holds for at least one popular system. Even the AI Snake Oil authors he was rebutting said training data is mostly copyrighted.
limitations: The evidence covers Stable Diffusion only. Primary records for Midjourney and DALL-E were not obtained.
The judgment came after the post, but the admissions are about training done before it.

our_interpretation: Plain reading: by the post date (2024-01-24), at least one widely used image generator had been trained on images that were under copyright. Whether that training was lawful is not part of the claim.
A developer's admission in court, or a court finding, that a popular image model was trained on copyrighted images is enough to support the claim.
The aside 'nobody is really disputing this' is treated as color, not as a separate claim to score.
criteria.support_condition: A primary record, such as a court judgment or a company admission, shows that a popular image generator (e.g., Stable Diffusion, Midjourney, DALL-E) was trained on copyrighted images before late January 2024.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Reliable evidence shows that popular image generators of the time were trained only on licensed, public-domain or otherwise non-copyrighted images.
